raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old man, a primary school director in Ain Trik-Setif, followed by goiter in euthyroidism, was admitted on September 26, 2020 to the Infectious Diseases Department of the University Hospital of Setif-Algeria for acute febrile hepatonephritis. The interrogation did not reveal any notion of alcohol consumption or a journey to a malaria-endemic area; however, he participated in renovation work on his house one month before.
 The onset was one week ago, marked by a high fever, repeated chills, and diffuse myalgias, followed 4 days later by mucocutaneous jaundice, yellowish diarrhea (more than 4 stools/day), and abdominal pain more localized in the right hypochondrium. On examination, the patient was altered, dehydrated, and conscious. The temperature was 38 C, blood pressure at 90/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation in the air 98%. The jaundice was flaring and the liver and spleen were normal in size.
 The paraclinical evaluation revealed: white blood cells at 29 000/mm3 of which 91% were neutrophils, hemoglobin at 8.7 g/dL (normochromic, normocytic), and platelet counts at 30 000/mm3. On renal workup: serum creatinine at 76 mg/L, urea at 1.38 g/L, and on liver workup: alanine aminotransferase at 140 IU/L, aspartate aminotransferases at 180 UI/L, alkaline phosphatase at 194 IU/L, total bilirubin at 425 mg/L, of which 80% was conjugated and the prothrombin level at 95%. The lumbar puncture brought back a clear cerebrospinal fluid, and cytochemical normal.
 The chest radiograph was unremarkable and abdominopelvic ultrasound showed a normal-sized liver, non-dilated bile ducts, and low abundance fluid effusion.
 The patient was treated with ceftriaxone + ciprofloxacin + metronidazole + parenteral rehydration, in the hypothesis of leptospirosis or sepsis with a digestive origin. On the 3rd day, the blood pressure dropped to 60/40 mm Hg. He presented with moderate hematemesis and was unable to eat due to abdominal pain and nausea. The abdomen was tense and bloated but depressible to palpation. The transit was preserved and the diuresis was null.
 Biologically, there was a worsening of renal insufficiency (urea: 3.31 g/L, creatinine: 106 mg/L, hyponatremia at 115 mEq/L), a fall in hemoglobin levels to 6.7 g/dL, procalcitonin at 111 ng/mL, creatine phosphokinase at 833 IU/L, lactate dehydrogenase at 955 IU/L, lipaemia at 273 IU/L (normal value less than 67 IU/L), and amylasemia at 429 IU/L. Electrocardiography and echocardiography were without abnormalities.
 Abdominal computed tomographic (CT) angiography showed an enlarged pancreas at the expense of its caudal part losing the lobulated aspect opposite, slight densification of the peri-caudal fat, and a necrosis flow at the level of the back cavity of the omentums. Elsewhere, there was liquid digestive distension with a hydro-aeric level reaching 38 mm in diameter, a densification of the mesenteric fat opposite, and an intraperitoneal effusion of medium abundance under the subhepatic, peri splenic, gutters, inter handles, and pelvic level (Figures 1 and 2).
 The patient was transferred to the medical resuscitation service where he was put on noradrenaline associated with appropriate vascular filling, blood transfusions, extrarenal purification sessions, and Inexium. Antibiotic therapy was maintained.
 A gradual improvement (clinical and biological) was observed. The patient initiated a diuresis and his colors return. On the 17th day, the kidney and liver tests were correct.
 In terms of infection, blood cultures did not isolate pathogenic germs; HBsAg, anti-HAV IgM, anti-HCV antibodies, and HIV serology were negative. The search for SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA on nasopharyngeal swabs by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was negative. Martin and Pettit's (MAT) serology was performed on 10/17/2020, which was positive for Leptospira biflexa (Patoc strain) at 1/400.
 The patient was followed up several times, after his discharge from the hospital. No complication was noted.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old man presenting with a one-week history of high fever, chills, diffuse myalgias, jaundice, yellowish diarrhea, and right hypochondriac abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began one week prior to admission with acute high fever, repeated chills, and diffuse myalgias. Four days later, he developed mucocutaneous jaundice, frequent yellowish diarrhea (>4 stools/day), and right hypochondriac abdominal pain, prompting admission for acute febrile hepatonephritis. On hospital day 3, he deteriorated into hypotensive shock (blood pressure 60/40 mmHg) with moderate hematemesis, severe abdominal pain, nausea, abdominal distension, and anuria.
subjective.past_medical_history: Euthyroid goiter. Denied alcohol consumption or travel to malaria-endemic regions. Epidemiological exposure: participated in home renovation work one month prior to symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports chills, diffuse myalgias, yellowish diarrhea (>4 stools/day), nausea, vomiting of blood (hematemesis), and abdominal pain. Home medications: not documented. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: altered, conscious, dehydrated. Temperature 38 °C, blood pressure 90/70 mmHg (later 60/40 mmHg on day 3), SpO2 98% on ambient air. Flaring mucocutaneous jaundice. Liver and spleen normal in size. On day 3: abdomen tense, bloated, but depressible to palpation, peristalsis preserved; anuria noted.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: WBC 29,000/mm^3 (91% neutrophils), hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL (normochromic, normocytic; later decreased to 6.7 g/dL), platelet count 30,000/mm^3. Renal function: serum creatinine 76 mg/L (worsened to 106 mg/L), blood urea 1.38 g/L (worsened to 3.31 g/L), serum sodium 115 mEq/L (hyponatremia). Liver function: ALT 140 IU/L, AST 180 UI/L, alkaline phosphatase 194 IU/L, total bilirubin 425 mg/L (80% conjugated), prothrombin level 95%. Pancreatic & inflammatory enzymes: procalcitonin 111 ng/mL, CPK 833 IU/L, LDH 955 IU/L, lipasemia 273 IU/L (normal <67 IU/L), amylasemia 429 IU/L. Chest radiograph: unremarkable. Abdominopelvic ultrasound: normal-sized liver, non-dilated bile ducts, and low-abundance fluid effusion. ECG and echocardiography: normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: clear cerebrospinal fluid with normal cytochemistry. Abdominal CT angiography: enlarged pancreas at the caudal aspect with loss of lobulated contours, slight densification of pericaudal fat, and necrotic collection in the lesser sac (omental bursa); fluid digestive distension with air-fluid level measuring 38 mm in diameter, mesenteric fat stranding, and moderate intraperitoneal effusion in subhepatic, perisplenic, paracolic gutters, inter-loop, and pelvic regions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed leptospirosis (Weil's disease) presenting with acute anuric hepatonephritis, acute necrotizing pancreatitis, severe thrombocytopenia, septic shock, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding (hematemesis). Confirmed by Martin and Pettit microscopic agglutination test (MAT) positive for Leptospira biflexa (Patoc strain) at a titer of 1/400 on 10/17/2020. Differential diagnoses ruled out: blood cultures negative; serologies negative for Hepatitis B (HBsAg), Hepatitis A (anti-HAV IgM), Hepatitis C (anti-HCV), and HIV; SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal RT-PCR negative; malaria excluded.
Plan & Treatment: Intravenous ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole; transfer to intensive care unit for norepinephrine infusion, aggressive crystalloid volume resuscitation, packed red blood cell transfusions, renal replacement therapy (extrarenal purification / hemodialysis), and IV esomeprazole (Inexium).
Outcome: Gradual clinical and laboratory improvement with return of diuresis; liver and kidney function tests normalized by hospital day 17; discharged with complete recovery and no complications on follow-up.
